A cassette is a small, sealed case — usually made of plastic — that holds some kind of material (most often a thin magnetic tape) neatly wound inside it. The whole point of a cassette is that it packages something fragile or messy into a tidy, self-contained unit that you can easily slot into a machine, use, and take out again — without ever having to touch or handle the delicate material inside directly.

Think of it like this: instead of handing someone a loose roll of thread that could tangle, you give them a bobbin — everything is neatly contained, protected, and ready to use. A cassette does the same job for tape.
The core idea: a case that holds tape between two spools

Inside almost every cassette, you'll find a thin ribbon of tape wound around two small spools (also called reels). When the cassette is inserted into a machine, the machine's mechanism grabs the tape and moves it from one spool to the other — past a reading or writing head — and then the process reverses to "rewind." The hard plastic shell of the cassette protects the tape at all times; the tape is never fully exposed, only a tiny portion peeks out through a small window-like opening where the machine accesses it.
The most famous type: the audio cassette

When most people hear the word "cassette," they picture the audio cassette (also called the compact cassette). This is a small, flat, rectangular plastic case — roughly the size of a playing card but thicker — containing magnetic tape. You insert it into a cassette player or a cassette recorder, and the machine reads the magnetic patterns on the tape to produce sound, or writes new magnetic patterns to record sound.

Audio cassettes were hugely popular from the late 1960s through the 1990s for listening to music, recording songs off the radio, making mixtapes for friends, recording interviews, dictating notes, and much more. They were eventually replaced by CDs and then digital music files, but they have seen a genuine revival in recent years — many musicians release music on cassette today, and people collect them the way others collect vinyl records.

An important feature of the audio cassette is that it has two sides — "Side A" and "Side B." When the tape runs out on one side, you flip the cassette over and play or record on the other side. Each side typically holds about 30–45 minutes of audio (so a standard cassette holds 60 or 90 minutes total).

A video cassette works on the same principle as an audio cassette, but it is significantly larger and holds much more tape, because video requires storing far more information than audio alone. The most well-known format was VHS (Video Home System), which dominated home entertainment from the late 1970s through the 1990s. You would insert a VHS cassette into a VCR (Video Cassette Recorder) to watch a movie or record a TV programme.

Betamax was another video cassette format that competed with VHS and ultimately lost the format war. Video cassettes were replaced by DVDs and later by streaming services.

In photography, a film cassette (also called a film cartridge or film canister) is a light-tight container that holds a roll of photographic film. The most common type is the 35mm film cassette, which you load into a film camera. The cassette keeps the film completely sealed from light (which would ruin it) and releases it only the exact amount needed for each photograph. Once all the frames are exposed, you remove the cassette and send it to be developed. Film cassettes are still used today by photographers who shoot on film.

In older computers: Early home computers (before floppy disks became common) used cassettes to store data and programs. You would connect a regular audio cassette recorder to a computer, and the computer would save data as sound signals onto the tape — a slow but cheap method of storage.

In printers and typewriters: Some machines use an ink ribbon cassette — a case containing an inked ribbon that the machine strikes to transfer ink onto paper. Even today, some label-makers and receipt printers use ribbon or ink cassettes.

In cycling: A cassette refers to the cluster of multiple sprocket gears mounted on the rear wheel hub of a bicycle. This is a completely unrelated use of the word — here, "cassette" just means a modular, removable unit of stacked gear rings. It shares the word because the concept of a self-contained, removable module applies here too.

In construction and architecture: Prefabricated wall or ceiling panels — designed to clip into a structural frame and be replaced individually — are sometimes called cassettes. The idea again is a modular unit that slots neatly into a larger system.
What ties all these meanings together

No matter the context, a cassette always refers to a self-contained, often removable unit or module — something designed to hold a specific material or set of components neatly, protect it from the outside environment, and make it easy to insert into and remove from a machine or system. The word carries an implied sense of convenience, neatness, and replaceability. Whether it holds magnetic tape, film, ink, or bicycle gears, the object is always designed so you don't have to interact with the sensitive inner workings directly — you just handle the case.
Quick summary of all its meanings at a glance

• Audio cassette — holds magnetic tape for recording/playing sound
  • Video cassette — holds magnetic tape for recording/playing video
  • Film cassette — holds photographic film for cameras
  • Data cassette — holds magnetic tape for storing computer data
  • Ink ribbon cassette — holds an ink ribbon for printers or typewriters
  • Bicycle cassette — the cluster of sprocket gears on a rear bike wheel
  • Architectural cassette — a prefabricated panel or modular unit in construction
